title: One breath, one hiss, and the short a in disguise

slides.heading: Two letters, one vowel, two spellings of it
body: Two consonants, and the second is nearly the first.
One new vowel, written two ways.
The best shortcut in the writing system, and it is short.

slides.heading: An elephant and a chain, which are one job
body: Both low class, so both harbour.
The second letter is the first with a notch in it.
The notch is a link of chain.

slides.heading: Pen and paper, again
body: Real paper, a real pen.
Today's pair is nearly identical. The hand separates them.
Out loud, both halves of the name, every time.

slides.heading: The elephant
body: Its name is the sound, then a word beginning with that sound.
The word means *elephant*.
Your palm should move. This one is thrown out on breath.

slides.heading: What the elephant is for
body: Boats come out of the water on a chain.
The elephant is what pulls the chain.
One boat at a time, and nobody hurries him.

slides.heading: The sound he makes when the work is done
body: Work done, trunk up, one burst of breath.
A smooth climbing stroke with a tail flicking up past the line.

slides.heading: The elephant's letter
body: One climbing stroke, smooth the whole way.
A tail flicking up past the top line.

slides.heading: Write the elephant
body: **Start at the head**, top left, clockwise.
The climb runs **smooth and unbroken**.
A tail flicking up past the top line. Out loud, every time.

slides.heading: The chain
body: Its name is the sound, then a word beginning with that sound.
The word means *chain*.
A flat hiss. Air escaping, not air thrown.

slides.heading: Snagged, slack and sliding
body: Snagged, slack, sliding back into the water.
Sliding over wet stone is a long flat hiss.
The link that snags on the bollard is the notch.

slides.heading: The chain's letter
body: The elephant's letter with a notch dented into the climb.
The same tail above. The notch is the whole difference.

slides.heading: And the chain, on the same page
body: Head, climb, tail — then one notch in the climb.
Write it **directly under** the elephant. Compare your own two.
The letters are near twins. The names are not.

slides.prompt: The two letters differ by one detail. Name it, and say which of the two carries it.

answers: The notch dented into the climbing stroke.
The chain has it. The elephant runs smooth.

slides.heading: Somebody new in the back yard
body: The house again, and the back yard.
The back yard is where a vowel written *after* its consonant lodges.

slides.heading: The one who ends the visit
body: The name means *to press*, or *to compress*.
Two small hooks, written just after the consonant.
Where he turns up, the vowel is short.

slides.heading: The best shortcut you will get
body: Every vowel is long or short, and it changes the word.
**If he is on the end, it is short.** Every time, no exceptions.
**If he is absent, you have learned nothing.** It runs one way.

slides.heading: And here is the proof, one slide later
body: Same lodger as last lesson, same sound, and short.
No sign of the shortener on him. Short anyway.
**The flick is the length.** With it long, without it short.

slides.heading: Read this one
body: Chicken, short vowel above, mouse closing it.
**Say it aloud before you turn it over.**

slides.heading: That one
body: **กิน** — to eat.

slides.heading: Write the vowel, both of its shapes
body: Never written alone. Always with a consonant.
Two hooks after, or the small mark above.
Say the **syllable** out loud, not the vowel's name.

slides.heading: When the back yard is taken
body: A final consonant stands in the back yard too, and gets there first.
So the vowel climbs: one curl, written above the first letter.
Same sound, same length. Only the seat changed.

slides.heading: Three of them
body: *together*, *loud*, *to measure*.
All three: short vowel, final consonant, curl on the roof.

slides.heading: Write the climb
body: The curl goes above the first letter, not behind it.
Write it beside the two-hooks version.
**They sound the same.** Only the seat changed.

slides.heading: Low class, stopped short
body: Low class, short vowel, dead ending: the pitch jumps high.
Both of those are sealed by a real final consonant.
A short vowel with **nothing after it** counts as stopped too.

slides.heading: The same letter, ending live
body: Both open on the elephant's letter, which is low class.
Both end on a hum, so both are live, so both land flat.
Same letter, two tones. The ending decides.

slides.prompt: Two words open on the same low class letter. One lands flat and one lands high. Say which is which, and name the two things that decide it.

answers: Flat: ends on a hum, so live. Low class plus live is mid.
High: short vowel, nothing after it, so dead.
The class was the same. Length and ending decided.

slides.heading: Four lessons in
body: Ten letters, two districts, three rooms of the house.
A third of the vowels tell you their length by sight.
Next: the cellar, and the same length trick again.
